newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania appeals for quick NATO admission.
newsitem.headline: Romania appeals for quick NATO admission.

text.p: Senior Romanian politicians and the Balkan country's parliament fired a volley of appeals on Thursday to back their last-ditch attempt to win early admission to NATO.
Former prime minister Petre Roman said Bucharest would doggedly fight for a chance to be among the first former Soviet bloc states to be admitted into an expanded alliance.

"Our efforts for early admission should be more professional and stubborn now. We must play all our cards well and right up to the end," Roman, chairman of parliament's upper house, the Senate, told Reuters.
Parliament issued an appeal to assemblies in NATO's 16 member states to support Romania's bid, saying the country would assume the estimated $4 billion cost of integration.
In Washington, Foreign Minister Adrian Severin said Romania was able and willing to pay the cost of admission.
"The price of being left out (of NATO) would be much higher for us. We don't want to pay that political cost," Severin told the U.S. Cable News Network in a live interview.
Severin was upbeat about the outcome of his talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday: "She (Albright) was very positive. She said she will consider us."

Romania is lobbying for a change in its image as a longshot candidate for NATO's first eastward expansion, to be announced at an alliance summit in Madrid in July. More advanced Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are seen as near-certain.
Bucharest has won backing from France, Italy and other southern flank members as well as from Canada.

But Washington has limited support to praise for Romania's progress since reformists pushed ex-communists out of office for the first time in seven years in elections last November. Britain and Germany have also been lukewarm.
Romanian media highlight the need to win friends in the West, especially in Washington, by stressing its role as a haven of stability in the volatile Balkans.

"The United States should no longer have to look for Romania on the map," the daily Adevarul said of Albright's words after her meeting with Severin. "The 'maybe' underlying (Albright's) words should both worry and mobilise Bucharest at the maximum."
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea will plead Romania's case next week with Alliance ambassadors at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
Thursday's parliamentary appeal, endorsed unanimously, stressed a new partnership with Hungary as a plus for Romania.

Romania earned praise from the West for signing a treaty with Hungary last year settling old rifts over borders and ethnic minorities. Bucharest says a similar pact with ex-Soviet Ukraine will be initialled early next month.
